title: Mimosa Hostilis and Mimosa Tenuiflora: One Plant, Two Names
summary: Mimosa hostilis and Mimosa tenuiflora are the same tree. Mimosa tenuiflora is the botanical name in current use and Mimosa hostilis is an older synonym that the dye trade kept. Jurema preta and tepezcohuite are its common names. It is not the leather trade's mimosa, the sensitive plant, or the pink-flowered mimosa tree of American gardens.
body: A dyer shopping for this bark meets at least four names for it, and three other plants that share the word mimosa. Sorting them out takes five minutes and saves buying the wrong material.
## The two botanical names

Botanists described the tree more than once in the nineteenth century, and two of those names stuck. **Mimosa tenuiflora** is the name botanical references use today. **Mimosa hostilis** is a later name for the same species, now listed as a synonym. Nothing separates them in the pot: a bag labelled either way holds bark from one species, and any difference between two bags comes from the harvest, the cut and the storage, not from the name.
The dye and craft trade in the United States mostly kept the older name, which is why this shop lists the bark as Mimosa hostilis.
## The common names

- **Jurema preta** is the name used in northeastern Brazil, where the tree grows wild in the dry caatinga scrub.
- **Tepezcohuite** is the name used in southern Mexico, the northern end of its range.
- **MHRB** is trade shorthand for Mimosa hostilis root bark.
## What the tree is

It is a thorny, drought-hardy tree of the pea family, usually a few yards tall, with fine fern-like leaves and white flower spikes. The part dyers use is the bark of the root. The outer surface is brown and rough; the inner bark is a deep red-purple, and that inner layer holds the tannins and the color. [What tannins do in a dye bath](/blog/what-tannins-do-in-a-dye-bath) explains why that matters on wool and silk.
## Three plants it is not

| Name on the label | What it is | Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mimosa, in a leather catalog | Black wattle, Acacia mearnsii | A tanning material that gives tan and brown on hide |
| Sensitive plant | Mimosa pudica | A small houseplant whose leaves fold when touched |
| Mimosa tree, silk tree | Albizia julibrissin | A garden tree with pink flowers, common in the American South |

None of these gives the rose, plum and purple range this bark is bought for. The leather trade's mimosa is the one most often confused with it, because both are sold to craftspeople as a tannin-rich powder. [Mimosa hostilis compared with cutch, oak gall and quebracho](/blog/mimosa-hostilis-vs-cutch-oak-gall-and-quebracho) sets the tannin dyes side by side.
## What to check on a label

- The botanical name, written out: Mimosa tenuiflora, Mimosa hostilis, or both.
- The part: root bark, not stem bark and not whole root.
- The cut: powder, shredded, or whole pieces.
- The net weight and a batch code.
- A clear not for human consumption statement. This is a dye and craft material.

[Reading a root bark label line by line](/blog/reading-a-label-line-by-line) goes through each of those in turn, and [the three cuts of Mimosa root bark](/blog/the-three-cuts-of-mimosa-root-bark) covers which cut suits which job.

title: Dyeing Cotton and Linen With Mimosa Hostilis Root Bark
summary: Cotton and linen take Mimosa hostilis paler and browner than wool does, because plant fibers have no protein for the tannins to grip. Scour with soda ash, give the cloth a tannin bath, mordant with aluminum acetate or alum, then dye at a full pound of bark per pound of dry fabric and let it cool in the pot overnight.
body: Wool forgives a great deal. Cotton and linen do not, and most disappointing results on plant fiber come from skipping the preparation rather than from anything that happens in the dye pot. The four steps below are the standard sequence for any tannin dye on cellulose.
## Why plant fiber behaves differently

The tannins in the bark bond directly to the protein in wool and silk. Cotton, linen and hemp are cellulose, which offers the tannin far less to hold. The color still lands, but lighter, and it leans toward dusty rose, mauve and brown rather than the deep plum wool gives from the same bath. [Wool, silk, cotton and linen in the same bath](/blog/wool-silk-cotton-and-linen-in-the-same-bath) shows the gap on one set of swatches.
## Step 1: scour properly

New cotton carries wax, pectin and often a factory finish, and all three block dye. Weigh the fabric dry first and write the weight down, because every later amount is a percentage of it. Then simmer the cloth for an hour or two in plenty of water with soda ash at about 2 percent of the fabric weight and a small squeeze of plain detergent. If the water comes out yellow or brown, that was the wax. Rinse well.
## Step 2: a tannin bath

Alum will not hold on bare cellulose, so the fiber is given tannin first. Oak gall at 6 to 8 percent of the fabric weight is the usual choice because it adds almost no color: soak the cloth in a warm bath for an hour or two, then squeeze it out without rinsing hard. The bark is itself rich in tannin, so some dyers skip this bath, but a separate tannin step usually gives a deeper and more even result. Try both on samples.
## Step 3: mordant

- **Aluminum acetate** at 5 to 8 percent of the fabric weight is the mordant made for plant fiber. Dissolve it in hot tap water, add the cloth, and leave it for two hours or overnight. No heating is needed.
- **Alum with soda ash** is the cheaper route: alum at 15 percent of the fabric weight with soda ash at 2 percent, dissolved separately and then combined, with the cloth soaked for two hours or overnight.
Rinse lightly before dyeing. For the deepest shades some dyers repeat the mordant bath a second time.
## Step 4: dye

Use a full pound of bark to a pound of dry fabric. Soak the bark in cold water overnight, warm the bath slowly to about 175°F (80°C), and hold it there for an hour without letting it boil. Strain the bark out, or keep it in a mesh bag from the start, add the wet fabric, and hold the same temperature for another hour, moving the cloth now and then so it dyes evenly. Then turn off the heat and leave the cloth in the bath overnight.
Heat is what turns this color brown, so a thermometer is worth having. [Keeping a bark bath purple instead of brown](/blog/keeping-a-bark-bath-purple) covers that one mistake in detail.
## What to expect

| Fiber | Typical result from the same bath |
| --- | --- |
| Wool, silk | Rose through deep plum and burgundy |
| Cotton | Dusty rose, mauve, soft brown-pink |
| Linen, hemp | A shade paler and cooler than cotton |

A second dip in a fresh bath deepens plant fiber more than a longer soak in the first one. An iron afterbath shifts any of these to grey and slate; [iron as a modifier](/blog/iron-as-a-modifier-how-far-to-go) gives the amounts. Wash finished cloth in cool water with a pH-neutral soap, and dry it out of direct sun.

title: Scouring Wool Before a Dye Bath, and Why It Matters
summary: Scouring is washing fiber clean enough to dye. Wool carries lanolin, spinning oil and dust, and any of them leaves pale, patchy color. Soak the wool in hot water with a little pH-neutral detergent, without stirring, then rinse in water of the same temperature. Commercial yarn needs a gentle wash; raw fleece needs a real scour.
body: When a skein comes out of a good bath streaky, with pale patches where the color seems to have slid off, the cause is nearly always on the fiber and not in the pot. Dye and mordant cannot reach wool through a film of grease.
## What is on the fiber

- **Lanolin**, the natural grease of the fleece. Raw wool can be a quarter grease and dirt by weight, or more.
- **Spinning oil**, added at the mill so the fiber runs through the machinery. Most commercial yarn still carries some.
- **Dust, handling marks and sizing** on anything that has been stored, shipped or woven.
## Weigh first

Weigh the fiber dry before it touches water and write the figure down. Mordant and bark are both measured against the dry weight, and wet wool weighs far more than the fiber in it. [How much bark per pound of fiber](/blog/weighing-bark-against-fibre) uses that number.
## Scouring commercial yarn

Tie each skein loosely in four places so it cannot tangle. Fill a pot or basin with hot tap water, about 120°F (50°C), and stir in a pH-neutral detergent: a wool wash, or plain unscented dish soap, about a teaspoon for a quarter pound of yarn. Lower the yarn in, press it under, and leave it for 30 to 45 minutes. Lift it out, let it drain, and rinse it in water of the same temperature until no suds remain.
## Scouring raw fleece

Lanolin only melts in properly hot water, about 140°F (60°C), and it settles back onto the wool if the bath is allowed to cool. Use more detergent, soak for 20 minutes, lift the fleece out while the water is still hot, and repeat with fresh hot water until it runs nearly clear. Two or three washes is normal. Rinse hot, then let the fleece cool on its own.
## Three things that felt wool

- **Agitation.** Press and lift; never stir, wring or rub.
- **Sudden changes of temperature.** Move wool only between baths of similar heat.
- **Running water.** Fill the basin first, then add the wool, so the stream never hits the fiber.
## How to tell it is clean
Clean wool wets out at once and sinks. Greasy wool floats and beads water. It should also smell of nothing much: a strong sheep smell from wet yarn means lanolin is still there.
## What comes next

Scoured wool can go straight into the mordant bath while it is still wet. [Mordanting wool before a bark bath](/blog/mordanting-wool-before-a-bark-bath) picks up from here, and [eight faults that spoil a first bath](/blog/the-faults-that-spoil-a-first-bath) lists the other common causes of uneven color. Cotton and linen need a different scour, with soda ash at a simmer; [dyeing cotton and linen with Mimosa hostilis](/blog/dyeing-cotton-and-linen-with-mimosa-hostilis) covers it.

title: Hard Water and Natural Dyes: What Your Tap Does to the Shade
summary: Hard water carries calcium and magnesium and usually runs alkaline, and both shift a tannin dye. With Mimosa hostilis the purples drift toward brown and the color looks duller. Iron in well water greys it further. Rainwater or distilled water is the simplest answer; a little white vinegar or citric acid, to bring the bath to about pH 5 or 6, is the next best.
body: Two dyers can follow the same notes with bark from the same bag and get different colors. When that happens the difference is usually the water. It is the largest ingredient in the pot and the one nobody weighs.
## What hard water is
Hardness is dissolved calcium and magnesium, picked up as water passes through limestone and chalk. The U.S. Geological Survey sorts it into four bands, measured as calcium carbonate:

| Band | Milligrams per liter |
| --- | --- |
| Soft | 0 to 60 |
| Moderately hard | 61 to 120 |
| Hard | 121 to 180 |
| Very hard | More than 180 |
Your water supplier publishes the figure in its annual water quality report, and limescale in the kettle is a fair sign without one.
## What it does to a bark bath

- **It raises the pH.** Hard water is usually alkaline, and alkali moves this color away from rose and plum. [Using pH to steer the shade](/blog/using-ph-to-steer-the-shade) shows how far a small shift goes.
- **The minerals bind with tannin.** Some of the color that should reach the fiber is tied up in the water instead, so the result is paler and flatter.
- **Iron saddens it.** Well water and old pipes can carry iron, and even a trace turns a tannin dye toward grey. Useful when you mean it, unwelcome when you do not.
- **Chlorine dulls some shades.** City water is chlorinated. Filling the pot the night before and leaving it uncovered lets most of it escape.
## How to check your own water

Dip a pH test strip in a glass of cold tap water. A reading near 7 is neutral and fine to use as it comes. A reading of 8 or more means the water will push the bath alkaline. For iron, look at the sink and the toilet cistern: orange-brown staining means it is there.
## What to do about it

- **Use rainwater or distilled water for the dye bath.** Rain is naturally soft and slightly acidic, which suits this bark well. The dye bath is the pot that matters most; scouring and rinsing can stay on tap water.
- **Or correct the tap water.** Add white vinegar or citric acid a teaspoon at a time, stirring and testing, until the bath reads about pH 5 or 6. Do this before the bark goes in.
- **Keep iron out.** Use a stainless steel or unchipped enamel pot, and stainless or wooden tools. A cast iron or rusty pot acts as an iron modifier whether you want one or not.
- **Rinse in the water you dyed in, if you can.** A hard-water rinse can shift a finished color slightly.
## Keep a note of it

Write the water down with everything else: tap, rain or distilled, and the pH if you measured it. It is the detail most often missing when a color cannot be repeated. [Testing a dye before you commit a fleece](/blog/testing-a-dye-before-you-commit-a-fleece) covers the rest of the sampling routine, and the [state pages](/where-we-ship) carry tap water notes for many states.

title: Dyeing Wool With Sassafras Root Bark
summary: Sassafras root bark gives warm tan, rose-tan and orange-brown on wool mordanted with alum, and grey-brown with an iron afterbath. Use about a pound of bark to a pound of dry wool. Soak the bark overnight, simmer it gently for an hour, strain, then hold the mordanted wool in the bath just under a simmer for an hour and let it cool there.
body: Sassafras is one of the traditional dye trees of eastern North America, and its root bark is an easy first dye: it is forgiving about temperature, it smells pleasant in the pot, and it gives the kind of warm, quiet browns that sit well beside brighter colors. [Sassafras albidum, a North American dye tree](/blog/sassafras-albidum-the-north-american-dye-tree) covers the tree itself.
## What you need

- Sassafras root bark, about the same weight as the dry wool.
- Wool yarn or fleece, scoured and mordanted with alum.
- A stainless steel or enamel pot kept for dyeing, never used for food.
- A strainer or a mesh bag, a thermometer, and rubber gloves.
## Prepare the wool

Weigh the wool dry, then scour it so the color can reach the fiber; [scouring wool before a dye bath](/blog/scouring-wool-before-a-dye-bath) gives the method. Mordant with alum at 10 to 15 percent of the dry weight. Sassafras will color unmordanted wool, but paler, and it does not last as well. [Mordanting wool before a bark bath](/blog/mordanting-wool-before-a-bark-bath) has the steps.
## Make the bath

Put the bark in the pot, cover it with cold water, and leave it overnight. The next day bring it slowly to a gentle simmer and hold it there for an hour. The water turns a clear red-brown. Strain the bark out and keep it: it will give a second, lighter bath.
## Dye

Let the bath cool until it is comfortable to touch, add the wet mordanted wool, and bring it back up slowly to just under a simmer, about 180°F (82°C). Hold it for 45 minutes to an hour, turning the wool gently once or twice. Then switch off the heat and leave the wool to cool in the pot, overnight if you can. Rinse in water of the same temperature until it runs clear, and dry it in the shade.
## The shades

| Method | Typical color on wool |
| --- | --- |
| Alum mordant, full-strength bath | Warm tan to orange-brown |
| Alum mordant, second bath | Pale rose-tan, soft beige |
| Alum, then an iron afterbath | Grey-brown, taupe |
| No mordant | Light tan |

Water and wool both change the result, so dye a small sample first. An iron afterbath needs very little iron and only a few minutes; [iron as a modifier](/blog/iron-as-a-modifier-how-far-to-go) gives the amounts.
## Using it with Mimosa hostilis

The two barks work well together. A pale pink from a light Mimosa hostilis bath, dipped afterwards in sassafras, turns a warm rosewood, and a set of skeins dyed from both barks at different strengths gives a range of pinks, plums, tans and browns that all sit comfortably in one piece of knitting or weaving. [Overdyeing with Mimosa hostilis](/blog/overdyeing-with-mimosa-hostilis) covers the order to work in.
## Handling
Sassafras root bark is sold here as a dye and craft material only, not for human consumption. Keep dye pots and tools separate from kitchen ones, and work somewhere with moving air.

title: Overdyeing With Mimosa Hostilis: Purples, Rusts and Greys
summary: Overdyeing is dyeing one color on top of another. Mimosa hostilis gives rose to plum, so over indigo blue it makes violet and deep purple, over a yellow dye it makes peach, coral and rust, and with iron it turns grey and slate. Dye small samples first, and change only one thing between them.
body: One bark gives one family of color. Two dyes used in turn give a whole palette, and Mimosa hostilis is a good partner because it sits in the red-violet part of the range that few other natural dyes reach.
## How colors combine

Natural dyes layer the way watercolors do: each one filters the light, so the result is darker than either color alone and sits between them. Pale layers give clear mixed shades. Two heavy layers move toward brown, so keep at least one of them light.

| Mimosa hostilis with | Result on alum-mordanted wool |
| --- | --- |
| A light indigo blue | Lavender to violet |
| A deep indigo blue | Deep purple, aubergine |
| A yellow dye such as weld or onion skin | Peach, coral, soft rust |
| Sassafras root bark | Rosewood, warm brown-pink |
| An iron afterbath | Grey-violet, slate, charcoal |
Take the table as a starting point. Fiber, water and the strength of each bath all move the result.
## With indigo

Indigo is the classic partner, because a true purple is hard to get from one natural dye. Indigo needs no mordant and is dyed in an alkaline vat, and alkali shifts the color of this bark. For that reason many dyers dip the indigo first, rinse the wool very thoroughly, let it air for a day, and then mordant with alum and dye with the bark. The other order works too. Dye two samples, one each way, and keep the one you prefer.
## With a yellow

Dye the yellow first on alum-mordanted wool, then put the skein through a weak Mimosa hostilis bath: a second or third bath from bark you have already used is ideal. Pink over yellow goes peach and coral quickly, and rust if the bark bath is strong. [Getting a second and third bath from one batch](/blog/getting-a-second-and-third-bath-from-one-batch) explains how to keep used bark for this.
## With sassafras

Both barks are rich in tannin and both like the same alum mordant, so the order matters less. A pale pink dipped in sassafras turns rosewood. [Dyeing wool with sassafras root bark](/blog/dyeing-wool-with-sassafras-root-bark) gives the sassafras bath.
## With iron

Iron is a modifier and not a dye, but it belongs here because it is the quickest way to turn one bath into several colors. A short dip in a weak iron bath takes rose to grey-violet and plum to slate. Use very little, in its own pot. [Iron as a modifier, and how far to go](/blog/iron-as-a-modifier-how-far-to-go) has the amounts.
## Rules that save wool

- **Mordant once, with alum, before either dye.** One mordant serves both.
- **Rinse thoroughly between dyes.** Whatever is left on the fiber goes into the next pot.
- **Keep the bark bath under about 175°F (80°C).** Heat browns this color, and brown over another dye is mud. [Keeping a bark bath purple](/blog/keeping-a-bark-bath-purple) explains why.
- **Sample first.** Ten grams of yarn through both baths tells you more than any chart. [Testing a dye before you commit a fleece](/blog/testing-a-dye-before-you-commit-a-fleece) sets out the routine.
- **Write it down.** Note both dyes, both strengths, the order and the times, so that a color you like can be made again.
